Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: The inaction/self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. In a child victim context, 'not doing more to stop what happened' implies agency that is typically not clinically plausible for the same trauma profile; a more general shame/self-blame item would fit, but this specific omission-guilt wording is questionable.

Within the Threat node, 'difficulty concentrating' is not a threat appraisal but a general arousal/cognitive symptom. The other Threat items reflect current danger and hypervigilance ('strong physical reactions to reminders', 'need to stay alert to fall asleep'). This item weakens within-node coherence and does not match the node's formulation role as perceived current threat.

vignette: Tane had come to believe that the world had broken the day his caregiver raised the copper pan. It was a Tuesday, the kitchen air thick with the smell of overcooked potatoes turning black against the burner. The caregiver, wrapped in a heavy wool cardigan, had stepped forward. When the strike landed, the heat, the fabric, and the sudden pressure fused into a single, inescapable reality. For a long time afterward, the bruised skin and the lingering odour stayed locked together in his body. Now, fifty-six years later, the past does not merely visit him; it arrives whole, without warning, when a match strikes or a casserole hits the oven. Working as a detective in a precinct of Oceania descent, Tane's daily rounds are marked by a quiet vigilance. He sits in his cruiser with his shoulders braced, watching the street through the rearview mirror, never quite certain if the passing figure carries a threat. The precinct itself has become a landscape of familiar reminders. Last autumn, a new recruit handed him a file wearing a wool cardigan that matched the one the caregiver had worn during the worst of the beatings. Tane had stepped back, his pulse jumping to his throat, and had spent the rest of the week refusing anything of that heavy, familiar weave. He was certain that the fabric was a tether, pulling him back into the room where the pain had begun. What frightened him most was how quickly the world could tilt. A burnt smell drifting from the precinct breakroom would make him stop mid-sentence, his breath catching as if the air itself had turned to glass. He had learned to step back when colleagues gathered, the proximity settling heavily on his shoulders. When he did speak, he often lost the thread of his own explanation, his words fracturing before they could fully form. He would stand there, staring at the coffee machine, keeping his memories detached just beyond his fingertips, and a low, quiet rage would rise in his chest. The rage was not directed at anyone; it simply arrived whenever the memory settled over him. His sleep had been fractured for years. He lay in his quiet, divorced bedroom with the lights dimmed, counting the minutes, keeping his eyes open just long enough to confirm the dark was still just dark. His muscles remained coiled, reacting strongly to the settling of the house or the hum of the refrigerator. He had watched his own reactions in the mirror and had come to believe he was a lousy coper. He blamed his own character for the abuse, certain that his quiet nature and soft shoulders had drawn the caregiver's hands. The world, once predictable, now felt fundamentally untrustworthy, its rules stripped away as if they had never been there at all. Even when joy found him, it unsettled him. A colleague's laugh or a shared success at a crime scene would leave him standing at a slight remove, unsure what to do with the warmth. He had learned to let it pass without fully embracing it, as though positive feelings were temporary truces in a war he had not yet announced an end to. His avoidance had settled into steady habits, the kind that accumulated quietly. He ordered lunch alone, took the stairs instead of the elevator, and kept his desk cleared of personal photos. The consequence was not dramatic, but it was real. He had missed a partnership track, his steady engagement fraying alongside his quiet divorce. Tane finally walked into the clinic after a particularly sharp afternoon. A suspect in a holding cell had worn the same heavy wool cap, and the smell of burnt toast from the kitchen cart had hit him all at once. He had stood in the doorway of his cruiser, unable to move, feeling the old rage and the old vigilance pressing against his ribs. He was not looking for a cure, but for a place where his reactions could be acknowledged without judgment. He wanted to understand why the world still felt so dangerously close, and he hoped, however quietly, that he might learn to stand in it without bracing for impact.
